domain_setting: A busy supermarket and department-store retail setting; distinguish store types, floors and areas, displayed goods, customer services, shopping containers, staffed checkout, self-checkout, prices and promotions.
recurring_scale_anchors: five required layer groups: layer-backdrop, layer-context, layer-focal, layer-details, layer-lighting
no readable words or numerals; diagram-like symbols and price dots only
show a purposeful retail context when a word denotes a department, service or store area
use human shoppers for action/role cards and recognizable products for category cards

polysemy_resolution_table.beauty: A beauty and personal-care department within a retailer, despite the abstract Japanese gloss; not attractiveness.
polysemy_resolution_table.dairy: A supermarket category of milk-based foods, not a farm or dairy factory.
polysemy_resolution_table.produce: The fresh fruit-and-vegetable section, not the verb meaning to make or grow.
polysemy_resolution_table.line: A queue of shoppers waiting at a checkout, not a drawn mark.
polysemy_resolution_table.first floor / ground floor: The street-level entrance floor. The glossary pairs the regional names; show the ground-level store entrance without using building-number text.
polysemy_resolution_table.cart: A utility store cart for moving boxes and stock; distinguish from the wire shopping cart used by customers.
polysemy_resolution_table.bag: A generic grocery carry bag. Carrier bag is one store-provided handled bag, while shopping bag is a shopper carrying purchases.
polysemy_resolution_table.cash register: The complete checkout machine and money drawer.
polysemy_resolution_table.checkout: A staffed checkout lane with cashier, goods and conveyor; distinguish from the separate self-checkout kiosk.
polysemy_resolution_table.till: Cash drawer/register in the checkout group, despite the Japanese gloss meaning “until”; show the open money tray as the part of the till.
polysemy_resolution_table.sale: A retail promotion with multiple goods reduced, despite the general Japanese sales gloss.
polysemy_resolution_table.bargain: A single good-value purchase; distinguish from bargain-hunting across several shops.
polysemy_resolution_table.department store: One large retailer organized into departments; not a mall of independent shops.
polysemy_resolution_table.convenient: An easy one-stop store visit with needed everyday products on an unobstructed, nearby route.

existing_asset_triage.lesson_74: Scanned keyed lesson SVGs for exact and semantic candidates. Retain only direct same-sense scenes; reject exact-key images when the image context is misleading or too narrow.

glossary_context_notes: The catalogue lists 57 items, all initially TODO. The groups set the intended shopping senses where Japanese glosses conflict.
The “bag”, “carrier bag”, “shopping bag”, “basket”, “cart” and “shopping cart” terms are close; use different forms and use contexts to teach their contrast.

Batch 1 rejected the abstract beauty portrait, mall-of-independent-stores candidate and fashion-designer-at-work candidate. The department store uses a shared facade and visible product displays across several floors; the beauty counter emphasizes skincare/face care, cosmetics shows makeup products, and the children’s department is an apparel section with a parent and child.

Batch 2 reused the direct living-room furniture group for home furnishings. Rejected the utensils-only kitchenware candidate and the single table lamp because the targets are broader departments; the generic underwear image did not clearly teach lingerie. The new appliance shelf has powered household devices, kitchenware has unpowered cookware/dishes, and lighting shows multiple fixtures.

Batch 3 reused the clear dairy-food assortment. The larger supermarket has multiple stocked aisles and a self-service cart; the small grocery-store facade candidate is saved for its exact term. Rejected the single suit and single perfume bottle as insufficient department scenes; authored a clothing rail and multi-bottle perfumery counter.

Batch 4 reused the small grocery-store facade. Rejected the chest freezer and residential basement candidates because the chapter calls for supermarket sections; the new freezer is a commercial glass case and the basement is below street level inside a store. Reviewed two vegetable still lifes for produce; the authored counter and seller make the fresh-produce section explicit.

Batch 5 pairs street-level first floor/ground floor with the lower retail basement and later upper second floor; the highlighted entrance sits on the sidewalk level. Food court shows several food counters around shared tables. Elevator uses sliding doors and buttons; escalator uses an angled moving tread belt; exit shows a shopper leaving through an open door.

Batch 6 reused the clear handled grocery bag, and authored a hand basket without wheels to keep basket distinct from later carts. The second floor highlights the upper retail level above the street-level floor; shelves show multiple stocked tiers; line shows shoppers queued at the checkout.

Batch 7 draws the carrier bag being filled at checkout, a staff stock cart, a shopper carrying two purchase bags, and a separate wire shopping cart with groceries. Rejected the standalone changing table candidate because it lacked public restroom and caregiver context; the final baby-changing-facilities card shows a fold-down wall table, diapered infant and caregiver in a restroom.

Batch 8 reused the in-person customer-service desk; rejected phone support, the business-client consultation and a gym locker-room changing scene. Cashier centers a worker at the checkout, customer shows a shopper with a hand basket, changing room is a curtained retail fitting booth with mirror, and guarantee uses a product shield/check and receipt at the store counter.

Batch 9 reused the laptop online-shopping scene and cashier-free checkout kiosk. Rejected the toy-chest open candidate. The paired open/closed cards show the market entrance open with a customer entering versus its roller shutter fully down; convenient shows a shopper with several everyday product types close at hand along a clear one-stop route.

Batch 10 reuses the single-purchase good-deal scene as bargain, plus the register machine and attached product tag. Reject bargain-hunting and general discount scenes for bargain; reject the self-checkout kiosk for staffed checkout; bank cards and the postage-stamp album do not teach a store loyalty card. The new staffed checkout shows cashier, customer, conveyor and till, while loyalty card is presented at checkout with reward stamps/stars.

Batch 11 reused the clear thermal purchase receipt and multi-product retail sale image. The other receipt file is a duplicate; the business promotion scene does not mean a retail promotion. The new special offer highlights one featured item, the coupon is a perforated discount voucher, and till shows the register’s pulled-out coin tray.

Batch 12 authored the specific empty supermarket slot for out of stock and a premium retail boutique for upmarket. A final exact-key audit found customer service had been visually approved but not copied to the lesson; the face-to-face desk illustration is now rekeyed locally, and the final 57-card plan/build is complete with zero TODO.
